## About This Document

This document summarizes the keynote delivered by Provost Muscat at **Back to the Bay 2025**
on August 13, 2025 ("Back to the Bay Keynote Script – AI + Workforce Development," Office of
Academic Affairs, Cal State East Bay), and turns it into a practical **checklist for faculty**
in two parts: things to do to become more comfortable with AI yourself, and things to do to
bring more AI into your courses. The checklist items are tagged to the three pillars of the
Provost's upskilling framework — **[Fluency]** (AI Fluency), **[Human-Centric]** (Human-Centric
Skills), and **[Agility]** (Agility) — so you can see where each action fits.

## Summary of the Keynote

### Why This Matters Now

Higher education is standing at a crossroads. Several forces are converging at once:

- The **demographic cliff** begins in earnest next year: nationally, a 13% drop in high
  school graduates by 2041, roughly 1% per year.
- Over the past twenty years, **public confidence in the value of higher education** has
  steadily eroded (a large Gallup poll), across political lines, genders, and regions.
- Students and families are **debt-averse**: CSU East Bay graduates leave with about
  \$16,000 in student debt on average and take roughly 8 years to pay it off — a moral
  obligation to reduce.
- There is **no good replacement revenue** for declining enrollment, so resources tighten.

In concert with these forces, AI is **redefining what it means to be "entry-level."** This is
happening now, not later. Businesses will adopt AI for speed, efficiency, and cost savings,
and consumers will care less about whether a service is human- or AI-delivered than whether
it is fast, affordable, and meets their needs. Graduates will need to mature professionally
at a faster pace, handling more complex, judgment-based work earlier — so these capabilities
must be part of the college experience **from the very beginning**, not waiting until a
student's last year.

### Employer Expectations: Beyond Technical Skills

Employers want more than technical competence. They want graduates who can:

- **Think critically** — "Does this make sense in this situation? What assumptions am I
  making, and are they valid here?"
- **Communicate clearly** — explain complex ideas outside their field and tailor messages
  to different audiences.
- **Collaborate with agility** — work productively with both people and digital tools.
- **Adapt quickly** — shift direction when new information or challenges arise.
- **Exercise ethical judgment** — decide what *should* be done, not just what *can* be done,
  and anticipate and prevent harm (the Challenger disaster was a failure of decision-making
  and of listening to engineers who sounded the alarm).
- **Demonstrate professional skills** — manage time, meet deadlines, follow through.
- **Show curiosity** — ask questions beyond the assignment, seek new perspectives. One
  business person calls this **"peripheral vision"**: seeing what comes before and after
  your work and understanding it as a system.
- **Show relational intelligence** — build trust, navigate differences, sustain productive
  relationships.

These are not "soft" skills; they are competitive advantages, and they must be
**intentionally built** through group projects, community engagement, interdisciplinary
collaboration, and solving real-world problems.

### Skills Gap vs. Experience Gap

The **skills gap** is the difference between what students know at graduation and what
employers need — and AI is closing some of it (engineering simulations without expensive lab
time; market analysis in minutes instead of weeks).

But there is a second challenge: the **experience gap** — the difference between being able
to perform a task and being able to do it in the messy, real-world context of people,
deadlines, and shifting priorities.

- **Social work:** AI can generate a case plan from intake notes — but can the new worker
  sit with a family in crisis, build trust over time, and navigate community resources?
- **Arts:** AI can write a grant proposal — but can the manager listen to local leaders and
  shape a program that becomes part of the community's cultural fabric?
- **Nursing:** AI can suggest a care plan — but can the nurse comfort a worried family,
  navigate language differences, and coordinate an interdisciplinary team?
- **Engineering:** AI can design a bridge — but can the engineer present it to a city
  council, respond to public concerns, and adapt it to regulations?

If we close the skills gap but ignore the experience gap, we graduate students who can do
the work in theory but struggle the first time they are tested in the real world.

### The Three-Part Upskilling Framework

The Provost proposes a three-part framework for students:

1. **AI Fluency** — understanding how AI works, what it can and cannot do, and how to apply
   it responsibly. Examples: a biochemistry student using AI-driven drug-discovery platforms
   and validating leads in the wet lab; nursing students integrating AI diagnostic
   suggestions into a holistic care plan that considers history, culture, and emotion; a
   history student using AI-assisted archival research while still critically evaluating
   sources; a music student analyzing audience-engagement data with human creativity driving
   final decisions; an engineering student using predictive maintenance at a water treatment
   plant while recognizing false positives and knowing when to seek human verification.
2. **Human-Centric Skills** — the interpersonal and cognitive abilities AI cannot replace:
   leading a contentious meeting toward a productive outcome, writing a grant proposal that
   inspires action, mentoring a colleague through an unprecedented challenge, guiding a
   cross-disciplinary team where success depends on trust. These are forged in moments
   requiring empathy, judgment, and adaptability — we must design opportunities for students
   to practice them in real-world, high-stakes settings.
3. **Agility** — the ability to adapt quickly when conditions change, with confidence rather
   than hesitation: reframing a semester economics project after a major policy shift,
   reimagining a design when a material becomes unavailable, adapting a production when a
   venue closes. Agility sees change not as a setback but as an opening for innovation.

### Experiential Learning as the Bridge

Experiential learning is the most powerful tool for closing the **experience gap**:

- **Internships:** a CS student using AI to detect fraud — the deeper learning comes from
  presenting findings to senior leadership and translating technical insight into business
  recommendations.
- **Community projects:** a literature class partnering with a museum on an AI-assisted oral
  history exhibit, using transcription tools then applying human interpretation.
- **Research collaborations:** undergraduates joining an AI-enabled housing study,
  integrating statistics with on-the-ground qualitative research.
- **The university as a living lab:** environmental studies students using AI-powered energy
  modeling to recommend campus sustainability upgrades and presenting cost-benefit analyses
  to facilities staff.

The progression should be intentional and built into **every program and every year**: first
year, a small team designs a low-fidelity prototype for a real community need (a volunteer
scheduling app, a household water filter); senior year, the same students lead a project
start to finish with an external client. Students graduate with a **portfolio**, a record of
real-world collaboration, and the confidence that they have done this before.

### Agentic AI: What's Next

Today's AI is mostly **assistive** — you prompt, it responds. **Agentic AI** is different:
you set a goal, and it plans, executes, and even negotiates with other systems or people.
Examples: a marketing agent that designs, launches, and evaluates a full campaign; a legal
research agent that reviews thousands of case files and drafts a brief; a biomedical agent
that identifies clinical-trial candidates, schedules outreach, and prepares ethics-review
reports.

**Implications for jobs:** agentic AI reshapes the entry point into many professions. The
low-stakes tasks that once gave new graduates time to learn the ropes — cleaning data,
initial outreach, preliminary drafts — will increasingly be automated. From day one,
graduates will be expected to operate at a higher level: engaging clients, interpreting
AI-generated outputs in context, and making ethical calls when the answer isn't obvious.
Because agents interact with other systems and people, **mistakes can cascade faster and
farther** than ever before.

**Our response:** give students hands-on experience **managing** AI agents before they
graduate — not just using them as tools, but leading them as part of a team. Build
simulations where students set a goal for an agent, monitor work in progress, step in when
adjustments are needed, check for quality, spot ethical red flags, and know when to override.
(A personal example in the talk: an AI agent comparison-shopped a hot water heater —
gathering specs, rebate data, and reviews, identifying licensed installers, obtaining
quotes, and ranking options against the Provost's priorities.)

### Addressing Skeptics, and AI Plus

To those who worry AI could diminish authentic learning or devalue their craft, the Provost
is clear: this is not about replacing the humanities, arts, or engineering — AI's growing
influence makes the **human lens more essential**. Graduates will enter workplaces where AI
is already part of the workflow; if they have never learned to use it critically and
ethically, they will be at a disadvantage. Avoiding AI entirely doesn't protect students —
it is the riskier choice, leaving them underprepared and risking the very fear that a degree
may no longer be relevant. But that does not mean handing learning to algorithms: AI can
process data, but it cannot care about meaning, context, and deep human relationships.

That is **AI Plus**: not AI *versus* humans, but AI *plus* humans. AI does what it does
best — speed, scale, and pattern recognition — and humans do what we do best —
interpretation, relationship-building, ethical decision-making, and creative synthesis.

### The Provost's Two Asks

1. **Where could AI serve as an accelerant for deeper human interpretation in the work that
   you do?**
2. **Where could *not* using AI be an intentional choice that itself teaches discipline,
   focus, and originality?**

These are adaptive questions about purpose and what we value most in teaching and learning —
designing experiences where disciplines don't compete with AI but stand alongside it.

## What "Upskilling" Means

The Provost uses "upskilling" in a specific sense: **deliberately adding new capabilities
and mindsets that prepare students to thrive in unfamiliar situations** — a structure that
ensures they are not just learning content, but building the **adaptability, judgment, and
creativity** to apply that knowledge in unfamiliar situations. It is more than adding skills
to a résumé: it is helping students grow into confident problem-solvers who can learn
quickly, communicate effectively, and work across disciplines.

## Faculty Checklist

### Part A: Getting Familiar with AI Yourself

Before asking students to work with AI, build your own comfort. Work down this list at your
own pace:

- [ ] **[Fluency]** Try at least two AI tools hands-on this term (e.g., the university's
  ChatGPT/Edu account, Microsoft Copilot with Office 365, Google Gemini) — use each for a
  real task, not a demo.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Run **one of your own assignments** through an AI tool and grade the
  output yourself. Note what it gets right, what it fabricates, and where students would
  likely stumble.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Practice **iterative prompting**: give context, specify format, ask for
  revisions. Keep a short log of prompts that worked and why.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Learn the **failure modes** — hallucinated citations, confident wrong
  math, leaked assumptions — and build a personal verification habit (re-run code, check
  sources, recompute results).
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Learn the **privacy rules**: never paste student data, unpublished
  research, or personnel information into public AI tools; know what your institution
  licenses and what is FERPA-relevant.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Read your **campus AI policy** (and your department's expectations for
  attribution and disclosure) end to end.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Attend one **Faculty Development** workshop or talk on teaching with AI
  (the Back to the Bay series is a natural starting point).
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Read one substantial piece on AI in higher education or your discipline
  (e.g., an EDUCAUSE or discipline-journal article) and note two ideas you could use.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Explore **discipline-relevant tools**: for statistics and data science,
  AI assistants for data analysis, code copilots for R/Python, and AI features in
  Quarto/Posit tooling.
- [ ] **[Agility]** Keep an **experiment log**: one page per month capturing what you tried,
  what worked, what you'd teach, and what you'd warn students about.

### Part B: Bringing AI into Your Classes

- [ ] **[Fluency]** Add an **AI-use policy to your syllabus**: permitted tools,
  **disclosure/attribution** requirements, verification expectations, and privacy rules.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Design one assignment as a **paired task**: an AI-allowed version and an
  AI-free version, so students experience both and reflect on the difference.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Require students to **cite and verify AI output** (attach the prompt
  used, the tool, and a note on how they checked the result).
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Teach **prompting and critique** explicitly: a short in-class lab where
  students prompt, compare outputs, and identify errors.
- [ ] **[Fluency]** Add a **low-stakes AI micro-activity** in one unit (15–25 minutes) before
  scaling up to graded work — scaffold from low-stakes to high-stakes.
- [ ] **[Human-Centric]** Add an **oral or viva-style check** where students explain their
  work and their AI use in their own words.
- [ ] **[Human-Centric]** Include an **ethics case** tied to your content: algorithmic bias,
  data privacy, disparate impact — students propose mitigations, not just detect problems.
- [ ] **[Human-Centric]** Require a **two-audience deliverable**: a technical report plus a
  one-page brief a non-technical stakeholder can act on.
- [ ] **[Human-Centric]** Build in **collaboration with roles**: lead, reviewer,
  communicator — rotating so every student practices leadership and relational skills.
- [ ] **[Agility]** Design an assignment with a **mid-course change**: new data, a shifted
  requirement, or a broken assumption that students must respond to.
- [ ] **[Agility]** Add an **agentic-AI oversight simulation**: students set a goal for an AI
  agent, monitor its output, quality-check it, and decide where to override it — then
  present their oversight decisions.
- [ ] **[Agility]** Include one **experiential, real-client deliverable** (community partner,
  campus as living lab, or industry problem) where AI is an accelerant but students own the
  interpretation.
- [ ] **[Human-Centric]** End the term by reflecting on the **Provost's two asks**: where AI
  deepened human interpretation in your course, and where choosing *not* to use AI was
  itself a teaching decision.
